newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS - South African rate rise hits growth prospect.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - South African rate rise hits growth prospect.

text.p: South Africa's central Reserve Bank said on Wednesday it was increasing its key Bank rate to 17 percent from 16 percent, dealing a fresh blow to an already stuttering economy.
Governor Chris Stals said the move, effective November 21, was necessary given an unstable rand, rising short-term money market rates and the threat of higher inflation.

"The unstable conditions in the market for foreign exchange, recent developments in the domestic financial markets and the growing upward pressures on inflation all dictate a need for tightening monetary policy at this stage," Stals said.
Commercial banks are expected to follow suit with a similar one point hike in the prime rates to 20.25 percent on Thursday.
The increase in the Bank rate takes the rate at which the central bank lends overnight to commercial banks to the highest level since early 1992.

The move took many analysts by surprise. There had been a widespread belief that Stals would resist market pressure for an official rate rise, at least until a clearer picture emerged on credit demand and money supply growth at the end of the month.

"To an extent it was unexpected in that we thought the Reserve Bank wanted to let the markets sweat it out a little bit until they got hold of the next credit numbers," said Dennis Dykes, chief economist at Nedcor bank.
"But looking at it coldly with the rand still under pressure and credit demand still very high and the market shortage for this time of the month very high, it can't necessarily be criticised."
However, the move was condemned by the South African Chamber of Business (Sacob) which described it as a "severe blow" to the economy.
"The rise in interest rates at this time will have a negative effect on business and consumer confidence, will tend to reduce sales and generally put a dampener on economic activity," it said.
Many economists already expect growth to slow to 2.0-2.5 percent next year, down from around 3.0 percent this year and a seven-year high of 3.3 percent achieved in 1995.
Some said it was possible rates might be cut again in the first half of next year, given that credit growth -- a major concern of Stals -- already seemed to be slowing.

"I see this as a temporary situation and with the economy slowing down I think one can see a reversal, possibly quite early next year, if the rand stabilises at current levels," said Johan Louw, chief economist at life assurer Sanlam in Cape Town.

Shares on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange are expected to react negatively to the news when trading resumes on Thursday, although Stals softened the blow by announcing some good news on the country's balance of payments.

He said preliminary estimates indicated that, on a seasonally adjusted and annualised basis, the country's current account deficit had fallen by approximately six billion rand ($1.29 billion) to 10 billion rand in the third quarter of 1996.
Stals said the South African economy was now moving into a period of consolidation after three years of increasing growth rates, which should help the rand stabilise.
The currency has shed 22.2 percent of its value on a trade-weighted basis so far this year.

"During this consolidation period rates of growth in some of the more important macro-economic aggregates such as gross domestic expenditure will decline to lower, but more sustainable levels," he said.

Pressure for a rate increase has mounted steadily this month with commercial banks squeezed by a severe money market shortage, averaging over nine billion rand a day, reflecting lack of funds due to renewed investor uncertainty in the face of further falls in the rand.
